title: Citizen Science Air Quality Monitoring
overview: Citizen science air quality monitoring uses low-cost sensors operated by volunteers to fill spatial gaps left by sparse networks of official reference-grade air quality stations. A city might operate only a handful of regulatory monitors, while a volunteer network can deploy dozens of sensors across neighborhoods, parks, and roadsides.

sensor_types.name: optical particle counters
sensor_types.notes: estimate particle concentration by scattering light off airborne particles; accuracy depends on humidity and particle composition

sensor_types.name: electrochemical cells
sensor_types.measures: gases such as ozone, nitrogen dioxide, and carbon monoxide
sensor_types.notes: react with the target gas to produce a small electrical current proportional to concentration

sensor_types.name: metal-oxide sensors
sensor_types.measures: a broad mix of volatile compounds
sensor_types.notes: inexpensive and simple but cross-sensitive to many gases at once, which complicates interpretation

data_quality_practices: co-locating volunteer sensors next to a reference-grade monitor for a calibration period before independent deployment
applying humidity and temperature corrections derived from the co-location period
flagging or discarding readings that fall outside a sensor's specified operating range
cross-checking neighboring sensors against one another to catch drift or fouling
community_value: Beyond raw data, these networks build local expertise: volunteers learn to read pollution patterns tied to traffic, weather, or nearby industry, and dense coverage can reveal hyperlocal hotspots that a sparse official network would simply average away.
limitations: Low-cost sensors drift over time, respond differently across manufacturers, and are more sensitive to humidity swings than reference instruments, so most programs treat their output as a relative, exploratory signal rather than a regulatory-grade measurement.
